How making gives learners a public object for applying, testing, discussing and improving knowledge, and the three conditions it needs.

t: Technology is a means, not the learning outcome
d: A simple test for whether a piece of technology belongs in a lesson, and why the answer is often no.
Artifacts, talk-throughs and reflection: what each one shows that attendance does not.
The three required parts of a level, and how the number of levels in a subject is derived rather than chosen.
Measuring readiness directly instead of using age as a proxy: what that changed, and what it cost.

t: A makerspace is not a computer lab
d: Where almost all connectivity is mobile, what is missing is a bench, a machine and somebody who knows how to use them.

t: Why the music room is next to the electronics bench
d: Multidisciplinary work in a makerspace, and the three jobs it does that a single-subject course cannot.
Selling a real product to a real customer as enterprise teaching, and five ways it goes wrong.

t: What counts as a solved local problem
d: The three tests a solved local problem must pass, and why a technically excellent build can fail all of them.

t: Measuring what cannot yet be claimed
d: What an organisation should measure when a sceptical search finds no strong causal evidence that makerspaces improve livelihoods.

t: Why an Ecosystem Builder Has to Teach
d: Why DreamSpace Academy runs education itself: it is where the people who build and sustain an innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem come from.
The case for sustained engagement through the school years, without turning age into an entry rule for the STEAM programmes.
The Changemaker Journey, Definition of Done, pedagogy axes and delivery lessons that make up DreamSpace Academy's method for the STEAM programmes.
A definitional review of Challenge-Based Learning, its lineage, its framework, and the single feature that distinguishes it from project- and problem-based learning.
A definitional review of "changemaker", a movement term coined at Ashoka rather than an academic construct, deliberately ungated by design, and therefore uncountable.
A definitional review of co-creation across four traditions that use the word differently, and the feature that separates it from consultation, participation and collaboration.

A definitional review of communities of practice, the concept's origin as an analytic of how learning happens in practice, its later reinvention as a prescriptive management tool, and the critiques of power and harmony that follow from both.
A definitional review of Papert's constructionism, what it adds to Piaget's constructivism, why its author refused to define it, and whether maker education actually implements it.

A definitional review of cognitive apprenticeship, the premise that trade apprenticeship makes process visible while schooling leaves thinking invisible, the six teaching methods and four design dimensions that follow from it, and what the evidence base does and does not support.

A definitional review of the term entrepreneur, the fifteen elements that recur across two centuries of definitions, the six a leading review distils from them, and why the field declines to settle on one.

A definitional review of the entrepreneurial ecosystem, a concept that reached policy ubiquity in under a decade while its own leading proponents were describing it as tautological, under-theorised and long on component lists but short on causal mechanism.

A definitional review of entrepreneurship education, the about/for/through distinction, the intention-as-proxy problem, and an evidence base whose effects are small, dosage-dependent, and occasionally negative.

A definitional review of experiential learning, Kolb's synthesis of Dewey, Lewin and Piaget, the four-stage cycle and its two dialectics, and why the cycle and the Learning Style Inventory rest on entirely different evidence.

A definitional review of grassroots innovation, the two research strands that developed the term independently, the social-economy criterion that distinguishes it from market innovation, and the unresolved question of whether an aided innovation still counts.

A definitional review of what to call a mission-driven trading organisation, and the finding that "impact venture" has no sector standard, only one institutional definition, which places it by financing stage rather than by values.

A definitional review of innovation, a term with no authoritative definition, a literature that says so openly, and the one distinction every source nonetheless agrees on, namely that an idea becomes an innovation only when it is adopted and used.

A definitional review of how learning in maker settings is assessed, process versus product evidence, portfolios, self- and peer-assessment, rubrics and their limits, and the interview method for eliciting what a learner understands about an artifact they built.
A definitional review of maker education, its lineage, what the systematic reviews actually report as outcomes, and the persistent gap between its learning claims and its evidence.

A definitional review of the makerspace, why the term resists definition, what actually separates a makerspace from a hackerspace, a FabLab, a TechShop and a community workshop, and how thin the outcome evidence still is.

A definitional review of unstructured, self-directed making time as a distinct pedagogical mode, the names it goes by, the benefits claimed for it, the well-documented equity critique, and the finding that open and structured modes are complementary.

A definitional review of the organisational lifecycle, a descriptive family of stage models whose biological metaphor imports assumptions about ageing, decline and irreversibility that the empirical evidence does not support.

A definitional review of Problem-Based Learning, the medical-education pedagogy in which an ill-structured problem starts the learning, and the reason it shares an acronym with a pedagogy it is not a variant of.
A definitional review of Project-Based Learning, the five criteria that screen a project in, the progressive-era lineage, and the acronym it shares with an unrelated pedagogy from medical education.
A definitional review of social enterprise, a term with four competing definitions, no settled boundary, and a legal-form question that is separate from it in every jurisdiction.

A definitional review of social franchising, replication of a proven social model through a franchise-like agreement, the spectrum it sits on, and the quality-control-versus-local-adaptation tension that is the field's central unresolved problem.
A definitional review of the term startup, why the literature has settled on no single definition, and which variables actually do the discriminating work.

A definitional review separating Direct Instruction (a specific family of scripted, field-tested curricula) from direct and explicit instruction as a general teacher-led mode, and reporting the unsettled dispute over how much guidance a novice learner needs.

A definitional review of tinkering, the Exploratorium tradition, its constructionist lineage, what "low floor, wide walls, high ceiling" actually specifies, and why the literature does not show that tinkering alone produces conceptual learning.

t: Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET)
d: A definitional review of Technical and Vocational Education and Training, the term, its rival names, the formal/informal split, the record of dual-system transfer, and an evidence base whose measured employment effects are far smaller and less durable than the policy rhetoric implies.

A definitional review of "underserved", a relational claim about inadequate provision of a named service, distinct from marginalised, vulnerable and disadvantaged, and contested for locating deficit in the community rather than in the systems that failed it.

The second run of the campus first photographed in August 2024, and the start of the year that ended in a pitch day.
What blockchain is, in plain terms, and how a local skill can become a paid digital service.
DreamSpace Academy worked with the contemporary-arts festival where the climate sound project was presented.

t: In-school programme reaches Nuwara Eliya and Kantale
d: Empowerment Inside School extends into the central estate sector and into Trincomalee district.
Another site in the hill country, after Hatton.
A German corporate foundation that funds education and water projects in Sri Lanka visited.

t: Makerspace in the public library, opened by the President
d: DreamSpace Academy co-created it with the Municipal Council at the Batticaloa Public Library, and the President of Sri Lanka inaugurated it.
The closing showcase of the school robotics programme funded by a micro-grant.
The six-month full-stack programme opened again, fully sponsored and taught in Tamil.

The progression used in the STEAM programmes: a four-stage scale describing what a learner’s making is for (Explorer, Maker, Innovator, Changemaker). It runs across every subject in the STEAM programmes rather than inside any one of them.
One of the four positions on the Changemaker Journey. A stage answers the question what is this work for, and entry to each is condition-based rather than scheduled.
The first stage, “What can I do?” Encountering tools, materials, ideas and peers through low-pressure experiences. Open entry: a person walks in.
The second stage, “Can I make something?” Focused practice that builds dependable capability in a chosen subject, through assessed projects.
The third stage, “Can I make it better?” Applied inquiry: using capability from one or more subjects to investigate a real problem and test alternatives.
The fourth stage, “Can I make a difference?” Entered by producing a grassroots innovation, not by time served, enthusiasm, or finishing a course.
Someone who has entered the venture pathway on demonstrated intent and commitment, but has not yet produced a grassroots innovation. A candidate becomes a Changemaker by producing one.
Depth within one subject, attached to a course. A level is three things at once (a descriptor, a volume of notional learning hours, and an assessable artifact) and all three are required.
The number of levels in a subject, derived from the real capability thresholds between a beginner and independent practice, never chosen to match another subject or fill a column.
Depth, Independence, Complexity, Impact: the four ways in which one level is deeper than the level below it.
A block of work inside a single course, for example “Level 1, Unit 2 of 4”. Units organise delivery; they do not carry a certificate of their own.
A planned, ongoing line of work with its own aims, which runs many courses, sessions or events. The in-school programme and the STEAM programmes are programmes.
What a learner enrols in and is certified for: one subject at one level, with published prerequisites, learning outcomes, units and assessed work. A level belongs to a course, never to a person.
One group of people who start and finish a course or bootcamp together.

A coherent area of learning and practice through which someone can build capability. The published list names the domains currently offered or in development; it is not a permanently closed set, and domains may be added, combined or retired.

An earlier word on this site for an area of practice such as electromechanics, software, media or music. It described part of one building, and it is no longer used: the practice it named is a lab, a capability and a community of practice that can run in more than one place.
A learner’s record of depth across subjects (say, robotics at level 4, music at level 1, plus stage milestones) held together rather than averaged.
A recorded, never-graded checkpoint inside the Innovator and Changemaker stages: a field test completed, a user trial run, a community agreement reached.
A course’s entry assessment: direct evidence that a learner holds the prerequisites, however and wherever those were acquired.
Someone who stops before the end of a stage or course. Leavers and their destinations are meant to be recorded as carefully as completers. That record is not yet in place.

A process expert who guides a group to unlock its own insights, solve problems or make decisions. In a lab the role rotates rather than being a permanent post. A trainer is the content expert; one person can be both.

The job splits three ways rather than one: the organiser sets the challenge and its context, the trainer (the published source calls this role the teacher) is accountable for the content, and the coach works with the learner on their own work.
A paired, longer-term relationship attached to a person rather than to a place. It is the usual delivery form for venture-pathway support.
Structured, syllabus-following teaching, tuned to the maker model. One of the two delivery modes, and a first-class one rather than a fallback.

Unstructured, self-directed, peer-driven time with the tools. It is not assessed by default (a learner may later submit something made here as course evidence if it meets the criteria), and it is timetabled rather than left to spare time.
The Maker-stage frame: a scaffolded brief supplied by the facilitator, with the solution left to the learner. Narrow in method, open in outcome.
Sustained work on a driving question producing an artifact. It is the Innovator-stage default, and the only thing the abbreviation PBL means on this site.
Starting from a real situation rather than a syllabus, and running Engage → Investigate → Act. It spans the Innovator and Changemaker stages; the Changemaker stage adds real stakes to the Act phase.

Open, playful investigation of materials, led by curiosity rather than a set task. It is the research tradition behind the Explorer stage, whose frame is hands-on exploration, and it is guided throughout: the facilitator keeps it safe and helps when asked, without turning it into an exercise.
The standard adjective for how this education is delivered: hands-on workshop, hands-on learning, hands-on experience.
An Explorer-stage entry format giving access to tools, ideas and possible domains. Unassessed, and no prior capability required; places, safeguarding and practical conditions still apply.
An intensive cohort format, running anywhere from a few days to six months, most often around three. It has a start, an end, and a funnel.
A public occasion people can attend without enrolling: a fair, exhibition, open day, talk, hackathon final or awards night.
Two different things: a funded project, time-bound work agreed with a funder or partner, with a budget and an end date; and a learner project, what a learner designs and builds.
A one-off, typically one day, with a prepared agenda.
One meeting inside a course, bootcamp or school term. It is the unit that carries a shape: opener, taught content, hands-on work, reflection.

Seymour Papert’s learning theory: knowledge is built rather than transmitted, and it is built most readily when the learner is consciously making a public entity (something that can be shown, discussed and argued with).
Learning through a cycle of concrete experience, reflection, conceptualisation and active experimentation. It is where the requirement for a reflection at certification comes from.
Making expert thinking visible: the facilitator models the reasoning aloud, coaches while the learner attempts it, and withdraws support as competence grows.

Education organised around making things: the research literature’s term for learning by making. Cross-disciplinary by definition, and framed around a mindset rather than a set of machines. DreamSpace Academy calls the programmes that teach this way the STEAM programmes: electronics, robotics, digital fabrication, and music and media making, in schools and in the academy’s own spaces.
DreamSpace Academy’s programme that trains trainers in digital security for journalists, media professionals and civil society.
A distinct tradition, originating in medical education, in which an ill-structured problem is the starting point and the curriculum follows from it.
Technical and vocational education and training: the sector a reader will most likely file this work under, and the closest formal comparator to what happens here.
The completion standard. Assessed work must show six evidence states, in any order: Aim, Options, Made, Evaluated, Shared, Refined.
Evidence state: what the learner was trying to do, and for whom. It may have been settled at the start or discovered halfway through.
Evidence state: that more than one way of doing it was considered, and that a choice between them was made for a reason.
Evidence state: something exists. An artifact, a recording, a performance, a working system.
Evidence state: it was tested against the aim, by some means the learner can describe (measurement, a listener, a user, a run that failed).
Evidence state: it left the bench. Shown, performed, published, handed to someone, or taught to another learner.
Evidence state: at least one improvement was made from what the evaluation or the sharing surfaced.
The made thing itself (object, recording, software, performance or documented service). The first of the three sources of certificate evidence.
A structured oral explanation of the work at assessment: how it works, why it was built that way, and what was tried and rejected.
A short written or recorded account of the process. It is the third source of certificate evidence, and the step that makes an experience transferable to the next problem.
The hard result is the artifact. The soft results are the capabilities it evidences (persistence, judgement, collaboration, the ability to debug).
What a completed course produces. It requires the artifact, the talk-through and the reflection (three sources, not one) and it names the course and level, never a stage.
Work to which the Definition of Done applies, from the Maker stage upward, which is where certification applies.

A replicable community makerspace that a local partner sets up as a social franchise. The partner provides the space; DreamSpace Academy provides the design of the unit (the equipment specification and layout), the brand, the operating standard and a licence to run its programmes there. Written in full on first mention.
The generic sector term: a shared physical facility with tools, materials, expertise and a community around them, open to people who could not assemble any of that individually.
The keyword of the model: the surrounding conditions (tools, examples, expertise, introductions, first customers, peers) that make entrepreneurial and innovative activity possible.
A group whose shared work is how its members learn. Newcomers begin at the edge on real tasks and move inward, which is also a description of a working lab.
Several domains taught side by side. Real problems are not single-subject, people arrive through different doors, and capability transfers sideways between domains.

Science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics, the frame this organisation uses across its programmes. The STEAM programmes are the academy’s programmes in making, robotics, electronics, fabrication, and music and media making, including its programmes in government schools.
One replicated makerspace site, in the smallest configuration that can still deliver the standard. The local partner that starts it pays for it, equipment included.
A replication model in which independent local operators run the model under a shared standard, support package and identity, with social outcome rather than profit as the return.
What must stay the same across every site for a certificate to keep its meaning: the completion standard, the stage definitions, the safety rules and the assessment method.
The pooled library of tested projects, briefs, curricula and assessment materials that every site draws from and contributes back to.

The four things DreamSpace Academy’s education offers a person. They run as threads inside every stage of the Changemaker Journey; they are not a sequence and they are not the four stages under another name. Whether they apply in the same way to the academy’s other teaching, such as business, digital security, workplace and teacher training, has not been decided.

Income and work, read across three tiers of very different evidential strength. Tier 1: small income, a maker selling what they made. Tier 2: a sustained livelihood, by venture or by wage. Tier 3: work created for others, when a venture employs, contracts or buys locally.
Research and development, entrepreneurship, and business and financial literacy, woven through every domain and every stage rather than appended as a final module.
The first area of the strand, make it work. Systematic inquiry applied to something real: prototype, test, document, repeat.
The second area of the strand, make it matter. Turning a working solution into something someone wants: opportunity discovery, value proposition, a minimum viable product, and a pitch.
The third area of the strand, make it last. Costing, pricing, bookkeeping, marketing and operations.
Make something, price it, sell it to a stranger, and work out afterwards what the result showed. The cheapest way to put a maker in front of a real user.

A new or improved product or process that differs significantly from what came before and has been made available to the people who could use it, or brought into use. This is the general definition in the Oslo Manual (OECD and Eurostat, 2018), and it is the main rule for counting the organisation’s innovations. Something built but never made available or used is innovation activity, not yet an innovation.

An innovation rooted in a real community challenge, passing three tests, all of them: the problem came from the community; a real user who is not on the project team has tested it; and someone depends on the outcome.
The route from a person with intent to a venture that stands on its own: three stages, one thread and four support modes.
Stage one of the venture pathway: entry. Two routes in: discovered, where field workers find someone already doing something; or co-created, where a learner arrives through the Changemaker Journey.
Stage three of the venture pathway: turning a grassroots innovation into something that can keep running: a venture, a service, or a practice that a community sustains.
What is offered at and after the gate: co-creation, bridging, domain expertise, and funding. Available in any combination and any order.
Connecting a local problem to a non-local resource, and the resource back to the problem: introductions to funders, specialists, networks and international opportunities.
A venture that came out of a real community challenge, has a credible path to paying for itself by trading, and cannot yet do so without support. All three clauses are required.
The point at which a venture pays for itself by trading and no longer needs support. The event has a name; the graduated thing is simply a self-sustaining venture, or a business.
The general term for any new venture seeking a viable model, whatever its legal form: for-profit, non-profit, cooperative or collective.
The person who starts and runs a venture. Entrepreneurs are what an ecosystem is made of, and support is not conditional on having come through the academy’s own programmes.
Structured support for an early venture (space, mentoring, introductions, and sometimes capital) for a defined period with a defined end.
The life stages of an organisation itself (idea, start-up, growth, maturity, and what follows). A descriptive frame used to place an organisation, not a pathway anyone is put through.

The organisation this reference belongs to: a non-profit social enterprise that co-creates an ecosystem to tackle local socio-economic and environmental challenges through education, innovation and entrepreneurship. It was founded on 30 September 2018 in Batticaloa, Sri Lanka.
The futures that become imaginable for a community when its people, knowledge, culture and opportunity meet through co-creation. Emergent, collectively held, and never a fixed list.
The frame for people who came through the academy’s programmes and now staff or run them, and the name of one documented route out of the academy’s education.

What follows the academy’s education: an open set of destinations rather than a fixed list. Documented routes include building a venture, research and academia, activism and community leadership, employment and freelancing, staying to work for the academy itself for a period (Grow Your Own), and leaving, which is the least understood route of all.
Work on the conditions that let a divided community function: cohesion, information integrity, inclusion and trust. Here it is a lens across all three pillars, not a fourth pillar beside them.

A capability and a community of practice in one making domain: the people who share a craft, a facilitator who keeps the work going, and the equipment the craft needs. A lab belongs to DreamSpace Academy, not to a building, and can run at the academy’s own premises, at a partner’s site, online or in a MakerSpace. It is named only when it holds four things at once: the making domain, a named maintainer, a team, and a date the statement is true as of.
A DreamSpace site outside the founding location. That is the only sense in which the word is used here.
A content expert who teaches specific knowledge, skills or frameworks, including people the academy does not employ. A facilitator guides the process; one person can be both.
The person accountable for a lab. The title follows the accountability and moves when it does.
A residential or multi-day intensive, run to a fixed start and end date.
The written account of how the work is supposed to produce the result (inputs, activities, outputs, short-term outcomes, medium-term outcomes and impact), with the conditions each step depends on.
Education, Innovation, Entrepreneurship: the three domains everything the organisation runs sits under.
What this organisation calls itself: a non-profit social enterprise. The phrase describes a structure, not a funding position: it claims neither independence from grants nor dependence on them.

Everything a person needs to solve a problem themselves and to keep solving the next one: skill, tools, a network, capital, permission to act, a problem worth solving, and standing enough to be heard. The whole bundle, not the first item.
A relation, not a location: local to wherever this work is being done. Reading it as one fixed place makes the purpose untrue the moment the model crosses a boundary.
Who a piece of work is rooted in, and who bears its outcome. Scoped per project rather than defined once, and made operational by the first and third grassroots-innovation tests.
Inadequate or absent provision of a named service, relative to need. Incomplete until two blanks are filled in: underserved in what, relative to whom, so every project states its axis.
The method: building with a community rather than for it, from problem definition through to who owns the result. It is also one of the four support modes.
Co-learn, co-innovate, co-produce: what happens between people in the ecosystem. An open set, not a closed taxonomy.
The countable unit behind the goal of one hundred by 2050: a grassroots innovation for which all three tests hold. Rung four of the innovation ladder, and nothing below it.
The global goals adopted in 2015. Results are mapped to them so that outcomes can be read against a shared frame.
Six levels that are never interchangeable: inputs, activities, outputs, short-term outcomes, medium-term outcomes, long-term impacts.
Four rungs that are routinely reported as one: 1 a learner project, 2 a functioning prototype, 3 tested by a real user who is not on the project team, 4 a grassroots innovation.
How many people an activity touched. An output, not an outcome, and reported as such.
Capability measured at the start and the end of a course, tied to that course’s own curriculum.
Planned contact at 3, 6, 12, 24 and 36 months after leaving, against a livelihood baseline taken at intake. Neither is in place yet. It is what would make the “Earn” question answerable at all.
A claim this model is testing rather than asserting, labelled as such wherever it appears, most importantly the second tier of “Earn”.
A figure supplied by the person or organisation it describes. Recorded and labelled, never presented as a verified count.
What a result cannot show: sample, method, timing, attribution. Published alongside the result, not in a footnote after it.

DreamSpace Academy is a non-profit social enterprise that co-creates an ecosystem to tackle local socio-economic and environmental challenges through education, innovation and entrepreneurship. It was founded in Batticaloa, Sri Lanka, in September 2018.

t: Is “social enterprise” a claim that you do not rely on grants?
d: No, and it is not an admission of dependence on them either. The phrase describes a structure, not a funding position. The work has been funded by grants and partnerships, by revenue from the trainings the academy provides and from client projects by its media lab and software lab, and by the founders’ own capital. The relative shares have never been measured, so no ranking between them is claimed in either direction.

t: Where does education fit in the wider model?
d: It is one of three pillars, alongside innovation and entrepreneurship, and it is the front of the whole system: it is how capability gets built before anything else can happen with it. The STEAM programmes are one part of it; the academy also runs business and entrepreneurship, digital security and teacher training. It runs in schools, at partner sites, online and in the academy’s own spaces. A MakerSpace is one of the places it can run, not the place it belongs to.

t: How many labs and ventures do you have?
d: Neither number is published. A lab is named only when it has a making domain, a named maintainer, a team and a date the statement is true as of; a venture count would need a stated role and a stated population it is counted from. Until those conditions are met, a figure would be misleading.

t: What part of your model is not proven?
d: Whether this particular rural pathway produces durable income. That entrepreneurship contributes to economic development is well evidenced; whether this maker-to-venture route does the same, and at what rate, is a hypothesis, and the measurement work exists to test it.

t: Which Sustainable Development Goals do you claim?
d: Nine, each with something specific carrying it. Two came off the list recently: one was removed because the evidence did not fit the goal’s own definition, and one is held as stated intent because the outcome has never been measured. Both reasons are published.

t: What is MakerSpace by DreamSpace Academy?
d: It is a community makerspace that a local partner can set up and run as a social franchise. The partner provides the space; DreamSpace Academy provides the design of the unit (the equipment specification and layout), the brand, the operating standard and a licence to run its programmes there. The programmes do not need one: they also run in schools, at partner sites and online. Wherever they run, people learn by making things, working on projects and real local challenges, explaining and reflecting on their work, and taking on more of it independently over time.

t: Is it a school, a training centre, or a makerspace?
d: The STEAM programmes borrow from all three and are none of them exactly. They are not a conventional classroom and not a computer lab. Learners work with tools, materials and other people, explore interests, build real capability and work on problems that exist outside the room they are in.

t: How is this different from a normal classroom?
d: In the STEAM programmes, learners do not mainly listen and repeat. They make things, test whether they work, explain the decisions behind them, improve them, work with other people, and apply what they know to projects and challenges that have not been solved for them in advance.

The academy’s programmes in making, robotics, electronics, fabrication, and music and media making, including its programmes in government schools. Learners learn by designing, building, testing, repairing and explaining tangible work. Technology is one possible tool in that, never the point of it: a well-made piece of furniture, a recorded song and a working sensor all qualify. The STEAM programmes are one part of what DreamSpace Academy teaches, not the whole of its education. In the research literature, this way of learning is called maker education.
It depends on the course, the places available, safeguarding requirements and any stated prerequisites. Open Explorer experiences need no prior skill at all; structured courses use a placement check.

t: Is there a minimum or maximum age?
d: Placement is based on demonstrated capability, not age: age is not used as an entry rule, a band or a label anywhere in the system. Safeguarding and legal duty of care still apply, and an individual course may have practical participation requirements.

t: Does a learner need good school grades?
d: Usually not. What matters is what a learner can already do and what support they need. Where a structured course has prerequisites, a placement check tests for those directly rather than using school results as a proxy for them.

t: How do you decide which level a learner starts at?
d: A placement check looks at demonstrated knowledge, skill and independence. Prior learning counts however it was acquired (at school, at work, online, or from a relative who repairs things) and it does not need a certificate behind it.

The STEAM programmes: electronics, robotics, digital fabrication, music and media making, including term-based programmes in government schools. Beside them, business and entrepreneurship trainings, startup bootcamps and a startup challenge; media and information literacy, digital security and digital marketing; and workplace English, leadership workshops, training of trainers and training for school teachers. Software and AI are taught as well, and whether they belong inside the STEAM programmes or beside them has not been decided.

t: What subjects do the STEAM programmes cover?
d: The STEAM programme domains currently documented are maker and fabrication, digital education, AI programmes, AI with electronics, software and tech-entrepreneurship, creative arts, and fitness and sport. Software and AI also overlap with the academy’s digital skills training, and where they belong has not been decided. This is the current portfolio rather than a fixed structure: domains may be added, combined or retired. They are not all at the same stage of development, and the programmes page says which is which rather than presenting them as equal.

t: Does everyone have to learn coding or robotics?
d: No. A learner may come in through craft, music, media, art, sport, coding, electronics or another available area, and those practices overlap, with technology supporting work across any of them. DreamSpace Academy keeps the domains under one roof because real problems are not single-subject and people arrive through different doors.

t: What are Explorer, Maker, Innovator and Changemaker?
d: The four stages of the Changemaker Journey, the progression used in the STEAM programmes, describing what the work is for. Explorer is open discovery; Maker builds dependable skill in a chosen subject; Innovator aims that skill at a real problem; Changemaker is reached by producing work that came from a community, has been tested by a real user who is not on the project team, and that someone depends on.

t: Is everyone expected to become a Changemaker?
d: No. The stages describe possible routes, not a ladder everyone must climb. Leaving with a real skill, a finished project or a job is a complete outcome, and the system is designed so that every stage records its leavers and where they went, rather than counting only the people who stayed. That record is not yet in place.

A level belongs to a course, inside the Maker stage. It is three things at once: a description of capability, an expected volume of learning, and an assessable piece of work. It is never a label attached to a person: there is no such thing as “a Level 3 learner”.

t: How long does the journey take?
d: There is no single duration, and none is published. It depends on the course, what a learner already brings, the projects they choose and the evidence they produce. Progress is based on demonstrated capability, not on time enrolled.

From the Maker stage onward, work is judged against a published Definition of Done: six evidence states that must all be present, in any order. Certification additionally requires three things: the artifact, a talk-through of it, and a reflection, which may be written, spoken or recorded. Explorer work is not assessed.

The emphasis is on demonstrated work rather than a written exam or a single mark. A learner shows what they made, explains how it works and why they made the decisions they did, and says what they would change.
It names the course and level completed and the evidence used to judge it. It represents demonstrated work against a published standard, not attendance, which is why the standard is published.

t: Are the certificates nationally or internationally accredited?
d: Not as a system, and this is not yet settled. Unless a particular course names an accrediting body, a certificate should be understood as issued by DreamSpace Academy itself.

Trainers and facilitators, and one person is often both. A trainer is a content expert who teaches knowledge and skills directly and demonstrates safe practice. A facilitator is a process expert who coaches, asks questions, helps a group reach its own answers and connects people to others who know more. The balance changes as a learner becomes more capable. Guidance is highest where knowledge is lowest; structured teaching is a first-class part of this, not a fallback.

t: How are learners kept safe around tools and equipment?
d: Every course publishes its tool, material and safety requirements, and access to equipment is matched to demonstrated readiness and supervision. Safety requirements limit what a course may offer.

t: What happens when a learner struggles, or something fails?
d: Trainers and facilitators treat failure as information, as long as safety holds. They can add instruction, demonstration, practice, feedback or peer support, and work can be revised before it is assessed. One of the six evidence states is Refined.

t: Will this help a learner get a job or start a business?
d: It builds hands-on, digital, creative, innovation and enterprise capability, and enterprise runs through the whole journey rather than being added at the end. Small income is a realistic near-term outcome. A sustained livelihood is a hypothesis the academy intends to measure rather than claim, and the follow-up that would measure it is not yet running. Nobody is promised a job, a business or an income.

t: How do you choose which community problems to work on?
d: The problem has to come from the community, not from a competition brief or a funder’s theme. Learners investigate the situation with the people affected, test whether the response is useful to a real user who is not on the project team, and a prototype on a bench is never counted as a solved problem.

t: How can a donor or partner tell whether this works?
d: The academy reports activities, outputs, outcomes and long-term impact separately, so that each can be read for what it is. Limitations are published alongside results, and the academy treats documented curriculum, actual delivery and independently verified evidence as three different claims.

t: What is this model’s biggest limitation?
d: There is no strong causal evidence that makerspaces improve long-term livelihoods in settings like this one, not in the academy’s own record, and not in the literature reviewed for this site. The system is built to generate that evidence rather than to assume it, and the instruments for doing so are published.

t: How do I find out what is running now, and where?
d: Courses, locations and dates change, so the current timetable is not published here. For what is open now (including places, dates, language of delivery, any fees or funded places, and accessibility arrangements) contact DreamSpace Academy at info@dreamspace.academy or through dreamspace.academy.

t: What should I ask before enrolling?
d: Useful questions: which course and level, what it costs and whether funded places exist, where and when it runs and in which language, what the placement check involves, what tools and materials are provided, what the safeguarding and supervision arrangements are, and what a learner leaves with. A course that cannot answer these is not ready to be offered, and every one of them is part of the published course specification.

t: Is there support for learners with a disability, or who need another language?
d: Accessibility and language needs are handled per course rather than by a blanket policy, and they are part of what a course has to state before it is offered. Raise the specific need when you enquire. It is a practical question about the room, the tools and the facilitator, and it is better answered before enrolment than after.

t: How can a parent, school, donor or community organisation get involved?
d: By asking what is running now, visiting where that is appropriate, proposing a school or community partnership, contributing expertise, equipment or materials, or funding access and delivery. The route for all of these is info@dreamspace.academy.

t: Can this model be run somewhere else?
d: The programmes do not need a MakerSpace: they run in schools, at partner sites and online. A local partner that wants a dedicated space can set up a MakerSpace and run it as a social franchise, rather than as an unrelated space sharing a name. The academy provides the design of the unit, the brand, the operating standard and a licence to run its programmes there. What must stay identical is the completion standard, the stage definitions, the safety rules and the assessment method; the domains, language, timetable and problems worked on are set locally.
